finding: The live range of $100-$440 is too wide for one job because it mixes two: a belt alone and a belt with its tensioner. For a belt alone the bottom is about right and the top is too high; the top only fits when the tensioner is replaced as well, and a dealer-priced tensioner can pass it. Built totals for the belt alone (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2018 Hyundai Elantra 2.0L about $69-$226 (0.3-1.0 hr); midsize 2022 Kia Telluride 3.8L about $122-$224 (0.7-1.0 hr); truck 2016 Tacoma 3.5L about $73-$246 (0.2-1.0 hr); luxury 2011 Acura MDX 3.7L about $67-$162 (0.2-0.5 hr). The low ends pair an online belt price with a manufacturer warranty time of 12 to 42 minutes, and three of the four are less than most shops will bill for any visit; the four benchmarks start at $109-$154, so $100 is a fair floor. Nothing built or benchmarked for a belt alone passes about $300. The Acura total looks low because both of its times are warranty times; at the general one-hour figure the MDX would come to about $163-$242, in line with the others. If a job runs to the 1.5 hours one parts retailer's guide mentions for hard-to-reach belts, add about $60-$80 to the mainstream tops. Belt plus tensioner: three makers state a time that covers the tensioner. Buick bulletin PI1173 (2011-2013 Regal 2.0L turbo) allows 0.6 hr to 'Replace Drive Belt and Drive Belt Tensioner'; Lexus bulletin L-SB-0164-08 (2007-2008 LS 460, 2008 GS 460, IS F and LX 570) allows 0.5 hr for 'R&R Accessory Drive Belt Tensioner'; Chrysler TSB 09-004-23 (2022 Pacifica Hybrid 3.6L) allows 0.9 hr to inspect and replace the tensioner and serpentine belt; a Ram bulletin (09-008-20, 2020 Ram 1500 3.6L eTorque) allows 0.6 hr to inspect and replace that engine's hydraulic belt tensioner alone. None of these is one of the example vehicles. Using 0.9 hr with tensioner prices gathered in the earlier check for three other common cars, which are no longer the class examples: 2016 Camry 2.5L with an aftermarket belt-and-tensioner kit ($69.95) about $178; 2015 BMW 328i about $174 with an OE-supplier tensioner and aftermarket belt ($65.95) and about $335 with genuine parts at list ($191.01); 2015 Corolla 1.8L with a genuine tensioner and belt at list ($357.59) about $466-$502. A Gates belt, idler and tensioner kit shown for the Acura MDX at $157.01 gives about $265-$301 at 0.9 hr. So about $175-$500 covers belt plus tensioner, and a split into roughly $100-$300 for the belt alone and $175-$500 with the tensioner would serve a reader better than one $100-$440 range. How solid the labor times are: every low end is now a manufacturer-stated time for the example vehicle itself (Hyundai 0.3 hr for the 2018 Elantra, Kia 0.7 hr for the 2022-2023 Telluride including inspection, Toyota 0.2 hr for the 2016-2020 Tacoma, Acura 0.2 hr for the 2011-12 MDX), and the luxury high end is Acura's own 0.5 hr for the 2007-11 MDX, which also covers replacing the A/C compressor bolts. All of these are warranty times, the low end of what shops bill. The economy, midsize and truck high ends are still a general statement that a belt takes about an hour; GM's 1.0 hr for a 2013 Malibu or LaCrosse eAssist belt and 0.4 hr for a 2017 Silverado HD diesel belt bracket it. The Acura bulletin was read from a copy posted on an owners' forum, not from the NHTSA site. Parts cautions: the Gates belt used for the MDX low end is listed for 2003-2013 MDX on a page that names the 3.5L engine, and Acura's list price for the genuine belt shows as $82.33 on one page and $78.80 on another; one seller's fitment table for the Telluride Gates belt stops at 2020 while another runs to 2023. No tensioner time was found for the Elantra, Telluride, Tacoma or MDX. The Tacoma is a midsize pickup and no full-size truck parts were priced. This is an estimate, not a quote. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the luxury parts low is now the discounted genuine belt ($57.65) because the aftermarket page did not confirm the 3.7L engine; luxury built total about $82-$162. The Acura times were read from a copy of bulletin 10-035 posted on an owners forum, re-read and matched.
extras: A quote often adds the belt tensioner and its labor, bringing the job to about $175-$500 (parts seen: a Gates belt, idler and tensioner kit for the Acura MDX at $157.01; for other common cars, $44.67 OE-supplier to $159.77 genuine for a BMW 328i tensioner, $311.03 list for a genuine Corolla tensioner, and a Camry belt-and-tensioner kit at $69.95). Idler pulleys are often quoted at the same time; one retailer's guide says worn tensioners or idler pulleys add $80-$300. Also possible: a diagnosis fee for a squeal or chirp, shop supplies and sales tax. A belt soaked by a coolant or oil leak means the leak is quoted separately, and a failing water pump, alternator or A/C compressor pulley found during the job is a separate repair. Some engines use a second belt or a stretch-fit belt that needs a special tool.
